reconcile.note: Matthew Henry reads Exodus 34's formula as one coherent character, since God's judgment reaches only three or four generations while his mercy extends to thousands.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll decries the third-and-fourth-generation clause as cruel, while Spinoza treats the mercy formula itself as a human, Mosaic accommodation.

quotes.text: Compare these passages. The first, a dungeon where crawl the things begot of jealous slime; the other, great as the domed firmament inlaid with suns.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (1881), on Exodus 34:7.

quotes.text: as he believed that the Divine Nature was subject to the conditions of mercy, graciousness, &c., so God was revealed to him in accordance with his idea and under these attributes (see Exodus xxxiv:6, 7, and the second commandment).
quotes.attr: Benedict de Spinoza (d. 1677), A Theologico-Political Treatise, Part I (1670; Eng. transl. 1883), ch. II, on Exodus 34:6-7.

sides.snippet: a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth
sides.verseText: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, \"Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

sides.snippet: visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children's children, on the third and on the fourth generation.
sides.verseText: keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children's children, on the third and on the fourth generation.\"
